Article Title: Accenture CEO Julie Sweet makes a 'vacation request' to employees for this August
Article Text:
Julie Sweet asks employees to help deliver a strong fourth quarter

Why Accenture changed its vacation policy

AI remains a key concern for Accenture investors

Accenture CEO Julie Sweet is asking employees to think twice before taking time off this August as the company pushes for a strong finish to its financial year. In a rare one-time policy change, Accenture will allow staff to carry forward any unused vacation days into the next fiscal year instead of requiring them to use the leave before August ends. The move comes alongside Julie Sweet's call for employees to focus on winning new business and generating more revenue in the final weeks of the quarter after the consulting giant reported weaker-than-expected quarterly results. Accenture’s new policy will give its workers more flexibility while helping keep more employees available during the company's year-end sales push.In a memo seen by Bloomberg, Accenture CEO Sweet urged employees to contribute to improving fourth-quarter results by finding new ways to serve clients and generate revenue. "Our shareholders are counting on us to deliver a strong quarter in Q4 — everyone can contribute," Sweet wrote.“This means we all need to find more ways to serve clients that create more revenue in the quarter and to originate more sales (small, large, mega) to finish strong,” she added.According to Bloomberg, the company has also allowed employees to carry over unused vacation days into the next financial year, which begins on September 1.Normally, staff must use their vacation before the fiscal year ends.People familiar with the matter told the publication that the temporary policy change is part of the company's effort to keep more employees working during August rather than taking leave before their vacation days expire. Another person familiar with the matter said the one-time change is also meant to give employees greater flexibility.The move comes after weaker-than-expected results. Accenture reported a 2% decline in new bookings for the quarter ended May 31 and projected fourth-quarter revenue of $17.75 billion to $18.4 billion, below analysts' average estimate of $18.47 billion. Following the earnings announcement in June, Accenture shares fell about 20% in one day, one of the company's biggest single-day declines on record.The earnings report also intensified concerns that artificial intelligence could disrupt the consulting industry in the near term, even though Julie Sweet has described AI as a "tailwind" for Accenture's business.Bloomberg Intelligence said in a recent research note: “AI remains the dominant concern for services and consulting. Though management positions Accenture as a long-term AI beneficiary, tangible evidence that AI is accelerating demand is limited.”
Article Summary: Accenture will allow staff to carry forward any unused vacation days into the next fiscal year instead of requiring them to use the leave before August ends. The move comes alongside Julie Sweet's call for employees to focus on winning new business and generating more revenue in the final weeks of the quarter.

Article Title: Who is Gautam Rangarajan? Indian-origin strategist appointed to key role by UK PM Andy Burnham
Article Text:
Indian-origin strategist Gautam Rangarajan.

Who is Gautam Rangarajan ?

What will Gautam Rangarajan do at No. 10?

Burnham's government overhaul

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Indian-origin strategist and former BBC executive Gautam Rangarajan as an Expert Adviser on Structure and Process in a newly created role at 10 Downing Street.Rangarajan, who brings decades of experience in strategy, organisational transformation and media, is set to take up the position this week.Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive with more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting.Before his new government role, he spent more than 30 years at the BBC, beginning his career as a radio music producer and eventually rising to become the broadcaster's Group Director for Strategy and Performance.His experience includes developing strategy in rapidly changing markets, leading large-scale transformation initiatives and handling complex policy and financial negotiations.The exact details of Rangarajan's responsibilities are yet to be outlined. However, the UK PM's office said his appointment draws on his experience in corporate strategy and transformation.His role comes as Burnham undertakes a broader restructuring of the machinery of government, including the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.Rangarajan is expected to play a role in the planned transformation at the heart of the British government.Away from strategy and public service, Rangarajan also has a creative side. He describes himself as a professional choral singer and music producer, alongside his work in corporate strategy and organisational transformation.The appointment comes as Burnham reshapes his government following his recent rise to the role of Labour Party leader and Prime Minister.His administration has announced structural changes, including the launch of No. 10 North in Manchester and the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.While the full scope of Rangarajan's new role remains unclear, his appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.
Article Summary: Gautam Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive. He has more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting. His appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.

Article Title: In 2020, Minnesota funded a $1.918 million Shell Rock River habitat program; by 2025, it had protected or restored 588 acres
Article Text:
Shell Rock River Watershed District (Image Credit: www.shellrock.org)

A habitat program takes shape

Three properties protected

Wetlands and prairie restored

More acres than planned

A longer-term conservation effort

In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. According to a 2025 final report from the Lessard-Sams Outdoor Heritage Council, the program ultimately protected, restored or enhanced 588 acres of habitat in the Shell Rock River watershed, exceeding its original goal of 483 acres.The funding was provided under Minnesota Laws 2020, with the appropriation directed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources for an agreement with the Shell Rock River Watershed District. The funding was intended to support land acquisition as well as the restoration and enhancement of aquatic habitat within the watershed. The program focused on several types of conservation work, including acquiring properties, restoring wetlands and improving aquatic habitat. The projects were selected using conservation planning and monitoring intended to identify areas where habitat improvements could provide significant benefits.The Shell Rock River Watershed is a shallow-lake system that supports fish, waterfowl and other wildlife. According to the final report, restoration projects were targeted at addressing habitat degradation and improving conditions for native fish, waterfowl and wildlife.One part of Phase IX involved acquiring three properties: the Glenville Property, the Bancroft Property, and the Church Lake Property. The District closed on the Glenville Property in March 2021 and the Bancroft Property in September 2021. For the Church Lake Property, the District transferred the deed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources in December 2024 after acquiring and restoring the parcel.The final report says these acquisitions contributed to the program's permanent protection of 218 acres. Another 370 acres of habitat and wetlands were enhanced or restored through the program. Together, those accomplishments contributed to the reported total of 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.The program included several restoration projects beyond property acquisition. The Bancroft Wetland Restoration was initiated in 2020, with construction beginning in June 2024 and largely completed by the fall of that year. Additional seeding work was completed in spring 2025. Another project focused on Panicum Prairie, where habitat enhancement work was carried out across 300 acres. The project involved native prairie vegetation and was substantially completed in February 2025, with final work completed in May.The program also supported the Fountain Lake In-Lake Habitat Project. Work included additional rock reefs and rock boulder clusters intended to improve fish habitat. The report notes that Phase IX funds were used to expand the scope of this work after the District determined additional funds were available. These projects addressed different parts of the watershed's ecosystem, from wetlands and prairie habitat to aquatic areas. The broader aim was to improve habitat conditions while protecting areas that could provide long-term benefits for wildlife.The program's original accomplishment plan called for 483 acres. By the end of the project, the final total had reached 588 acres, 105 acres more than initially planned. The report attributes the increase to the addition of the In-Lake Habitat Project and the Church Lake Property to Phase IX.According to the report, all grant funds were spent. The final grant expenditure remained $1.918 million, while the program's final total including leverage was $1.9479 million.The work is intended to continue beyond the end of the grant. The Shell Rock River Watershed District relies on multiple funding sources, including a local option sales tax, local levy and public funding, to maintain conservation projects. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources will also maintain the Church Lake Property, which it owns.The program's results illustrate how a single state-funded conservation effort can combine land protection, wetland restoration, prairie enhancement and aquatic habitat improvements. Rather than focusing on one habitat type, Phase IX combined several projects across the Shell Rock River watershed. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored. The completed work represents a combination of permanent land protection and habitat improvements designed to support Minnesota's fish, waterfowl and wildlife over the long term.
Article Summary: In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.

Article Title: ChatGPT gave Google 'Code Red’, prompting co-founder Sergey Brin's return; Now OpenAI’s Greg Brockman is facing 'Red Flag'
Article Text:
Greg Brockman goes into ‘founder mode’

OpenAI witnessing a wave of high-profile departures

In December 2022, the meteoric rise of ChatGPT reportedly triggered a “Code Red” inside Google . The situation led co-founder Sergey Brin back into hands-on technical development. Fast forward to August 2026, the tables have turned, presenting OpenAI leadership led by CEO Sam Altman and president Greg Brockman (both cofounders) with what industry analysts are calling a major “red flag” of their own.A wave of high-profile executive departures is shaking the AI company’s front office at a critical juncture, as the artificial intelligence (AI) giant prepares for an anticipated initial public offering ( IPO ) while seeking to validate an $852 billion valuation.Meanwhile, citing sources familiar to the matter, a report by Axios claims that Brockman is getting more involved in the company’s day-to-day operations to contain disruptions. Brockman is said to be meeting with more customers and teams across the company than ever before. Brockman is said to be publicly framing the departures as a change in corporate focus.The latest blow came with the resignation of chief revenue officer Denise Dresser after less than a year at the company. Dresser, a seasoned software executive who previously spent over a decade at Salesforce and Slack, was recruited in December to spearhead OpenAI's enterprise commercial strategy against formidable rivals like Anthropic.Her departure landed just two days after longtime COO and senior executive, Brad Lightcap, announced his own exit after eight years, leaving key corporate divisions in transition. Her profile expanded significantly four months later when she took over operational duties previously handled by Lightcap. However, Dresser's abrupt departure compounds a broader pattern of senior leadership churn.For example, Fidji Simo, the former Instacart CEO stepped away from her high-ranking OpenAI executive role in July to focus on managing a chronic illness. Four other senior leaders, including former VP of Science Kevin Weil and CMO Kate Rouch, left the company in April. The exits arrive only months after OpenAI submitted a confidential IPO draft registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission, raising concerns among private market watchers.“The executives leaving OpenAI ahead of their IPO is a huge red flag,” noted Kevin McCormick, founder of AI startup SignAudit.AI, pointing out that walking away before a liquidity event suggests underlying tensions.“If the executives leaving aren’t being ‘made whole’ by the next company, it’s bad news for OpenAI,” McCormick wrote, as per a report by CNBC.Meanwhile, Dali Rajic – former COO of cybersecurity firm Wiz – joined as chief revenue officer. OpenAI also hired top AI researcher Noam Shazeer from Google in June 2026. He is a co-inventor of the foundational transformer architecture and former co-lead of Google’s Gemini models, and joined OpenAI to head Architecture Research.
Article Summary: A wave of high-profile executive departures is shaking the AI company’s front office at a critical juncture. The exits arrive only months after OpenAI submitted a confidential IPO draft registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The latest blow came with the resignation of chief revenue officer Denise Dresser.

Article Title: ‘10 online shopping platforms that faced most consumer complaints, non-delivery of goods top grievance; Rs 91 crore refunds in one year’
Article Text:
​10 online shopping platforms that faced most consumer complaints

Top 10 E-Commerce Platforms by Grievance Volume

Regulatory crackdown and refunds

How NCH complaint system works

Online shopping giants Flipkart, Amazon and Meesho emerged as the top three platforms facing the highest volume of consumer grievances on the National Consumer Helpline (NCH) in 2025, the government informed the Lok Sabha recently. In a written reply to the Parliament, Union Minister of State for Consumer Affairs BL Verma disclosed that Flipkart topped the list with over 1.33 lakh complaints, followed by Amazon with 91,248 and Meesho with 29,284. Quick-commerce and niche retail platforms also featured prominently among the top ten offenders.Operated by the Department of Consumer Affairs, the NCH acts as a single-window pre-litigation website. It currently supports 17 Indian languages and connects consumers with 1,853 partner companies registered under its voluntary "Convergence" initiative. This means that consumers can lodge complaints in 17 languages, including Hindi, English, Kashmiri, Punjabi, Nepali, Gujarati, Marathi, Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Maithili, Santhali, Bengali, Odia, Assamese and Manipuri, through the toll-free number 1915.* Flipkart: 1,33,000* Amazon: 91,248* Meesho: 29,284* Myntra: 25,384* Netmeds: 19,895* Zepto: 5,774* Blinkit: 5,102* Naaptol: 4,079* VLE Bazaar: 3,907* Nykaa: 3,405To curb unfair trade practices under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) imposed fines on 47 platforms, slapping collective fines totaling approximately Rs 1.12 crore (Rs 1,12,01,500). The minister highlighted significant enforcement outcomes through pre-litigation resolution.The minister said that the NCH facilitated refunds of over Rs 91 crore to consumers between April 25, 2025, and June 30, 2026, of which more than Rs 63 crore pertained to grievances in the e-commerce sector. This was achieved by resolving over 1,47,000 consumer grievances related to refund claims at the pre-litigation stage, he said. A total of 5.11 lakh complaints related to quick commerce were received on the NCH in 2025, all of which were disposed of, the minister added.Non-delivery of products was the single largest category of complaints in 2025, accounting for 79,818 cases. Other frequent complaints included delivery of the wrong product, denial of replacement or refund as per policy, delivery of defective or damaged goods, non-refund of paid amounts, deficiency in services, sale of spurious or counterfeit products, and unauthorised debit of amounts without consumer consent.Consumers can escalate unresolved e-commerce disputes through:* Toll-Free Helpline: 1915* WhatsApp / SMS: 8800001915* Email: nch-ca@gov.in* Complaint websites: consumerhelpline.gov.in, the NCH app, and the UMANG application
Article Summary: Flipkart topped the list with over 1.33 lakh complaints, followed by Amazon with 91,248 and Meesho with 29,284. Quick-commerce and niche retail platforms also featured prominently among the top ten offenders. Non-delivery of products was the single largest category of complaints, accounting for 79,818 cases.

Article Title: America is 'getting ready' to send letter to dozens of countries telling them: You can go with us or China, it cannot be ...
Article Text:
America to send letter to dozens of countries

‘To be part of everything is to be part of nothing’

The Chinese alternative

Why Washington is pushing this now

The United States is preparing to send a letter to dozens of countries, telling them that they must choose sides in the global AI race, according to a report by Reuters. As per a US official and a draft reviewed by Reuters, nations that join China’s competing framework will be excluded from Washington’s coalition, known as Pax Silica. For the uninitiated, launched last year, Pax Silica is designed to secure supply chains for AI models, semiconductors and critical minerals. Around two dozen countries have signed on, including Japan, Australia, South Korea, and Kazakhstan. But Kazakhstan has also joined China’s newly announced World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, raising concerns in Washington. The draft letter warns: “To be part of everything is to be part of nothing. Signature of the Pax Silica Declaration is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment.”As per the report, The draft letter, prepared by the State Department, is addressed to the 35 signatories of a US. "AI Opportunity Statement" signed in June. Those signatories include members of the non-binding Pax Silica framework, an initiative Washington launched last year aimed at securing supply chains for AI models, semiconductors and critical minerals amid its intensifying rivalry with Beijing, as well as other countries that have expressed interest in aligning their AI cooperation with the US.Roughly two dozen countries have already joined Pax Silica, including close US. allies such as Japan, Australia and South Korea, along with Kazakhstan, a key potential source of critical minerals. Kazakhstan's involvement has drawn particular attention in Washington because it is also the only country known to have joined China's rival coalition, a dual membership that Reuters reports has set off alarm bells among US officials.The draft letter makes the case that AI alignment cannot be treated as a flexible, à la carte arrangement. It states that "to be part of everything is to be part of nothing," framing signature on the Pax Silica declaration as a genuine commitment rather than a simple membership subscription, and urging countries to choose deliberately rather than trying to straddle both camps. Without naming China explicitly, the letter argues that Pax Silica membership cannot be held alongside participation in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with Washington's own. Reuters was unable to determine when the letter might actually be sent, or whether its language could still change beforehand, since the draft reviewed was undated.The letter is a direct response to a rival framework China has been building. In July, Chinese President Xi Jinping launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, positioning the country's open-weight AI technology as a challenge to US. dominance in the sector. The move reflects a broader shift in the global AI landscape, as Chinese open-weight models have made rapid gains against proprietary systems built by US. companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, intensifying the stakes of the broader technological rivalry.By pressing allied and partner countries to pick a side, the US. is aiming to limit China's access to resources in the broader race to build the most advanced AI systems, technology that could carry significant military and economic weight. Pax Silica itself is designed to push US. allies toward joint projects and coordinated export controls while reducing collective reliance on adversaries for critical minerals, AI models and the semiconductor chips that power them.The critical minerals dimension adds further weight to the standoff. China has previously used its near-monopoly over several critical minerals as leverage in a tariff dispute launched last year by President Donald Trump, who has since pushed to expand domestic and allied sourcing of those materials. Kazakhstan's June entry into Pax Silica was touted by Washington as a milestone, marking the first Central Asian country to join the framework and bringing with it substantial reserves of critical minerals central to advanced technology supply chains.Under the current structure, Pax Silica members gain access to shared investment opportunities in AI-related projects, while countries that have simply signed the AI Opportunity Statement have made a more symbolic commitment to a shared vision and common purpose with the US, according to the statement posted on the State Department's website. A US official told Reuters that the letter was drafted specifically to make clear that countries can't have it both ways, arguing that it is difficult for any nation to credibly present itself as a trusted partner within one technology ecosystem while simultaneously joining an initiative built by China to advance a competing vision for AI.
Article Summary: US preparing to send letter to dozens of countries, telling them that they must choose sides in the global AI race. The letter is a direct response to a rival framework China has been building. In July, Chinese President Xi Jinping launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, positioning the country's open-weight AI technology.

Article Title: When 'Godfather of AI' agreed with Elon Musk; said billionaires like him are right about future of work; but there is a big problem and that is...
Article Text:
Geoffrey Hinton says Musk and Gates are right about AI ending jobs, but warns the real problem is nobody left to buy what AI makes.

Why Geoffrey Hinton thinks the trillion-dollar AI spending spree runs on job cuts

AI will create new jobs, but Hinton says nowhere near enough to replace what it kills

Bernie Sanders warns 100 million US jobs face AI automation risk

Geoffrey Hinton and Elon Musk do not usually land on the same side of an argument. But asked whether the tech billionaires forecasting the end of work were being melodramatic, the Nobel laureate widely called the "Godfather of AI" said they were probably right. Musk has said most people won't have to work at all inside two decades. Similarly, Bill Gates has suggested humans may soon not be needed for most things. Hinton, in a discussion with Senator Bernie Sanders last year at Georgetown University, said those predictions are not fringe. They are likely.The catch is everything that follows. Hinton's worry is not that AI is bad technology. It is that the economy sitting underneath it was not built to absorb what is coming. He expects "massive unemployment caused by AI", and he does not think the people writing the cheques have worked through the consequences. His blunt line to Sanders was that if workers stop earning, "there's nobody to buy their products".Follow the money, Hinton argued, and the intent becomes obvious. Somebody has to recover the roughly trillion dollars flowing into data centres and chips, and subscription fees for chatbots won't cover it. The return has to come from selling companies AI that does a worker's job for less. Big Tech, in his reading, is betting squarely on replacement. The financial pressure is real enough: HSBC estimated OpenAI won't turn a profit before 2030 and may need over $207 billion to keep scaling.Hinton also keeps pointing out that this is a design choice, not destiny. AI could do enormous good in healthcare and education. What makes it dangerous is distribution. Musk gets richer, a lot of people lose work, and as Hinton put it, "that's on how we organize society".The standard rebuttal is that every technology shock eventually produces new categories of work. Hinton accepts the first half and rejects the second. Yes, roles like prompt engineer appear. No, he does not believe they arrive in anything like the volume of the jobs being erased. The old escape route mattered: a ditch digger could move to a call centre. Those call centre desks are the ones going first.He is careful about his own confidence, though. Predicting AI, he told Sanders, is like driving in fog, where the next hundred yards are clear and the two hundred yard mark is invisible. A year or two out, he can see. Ten years out, nobody can. At the Ai4 conference in Las Vegas this month, he went further on capability, saying AI could surpass humans at everything within twenty years, and probably a good deal sooner.Sanders has tried to size the damage. An report last year from his office estimated nearly 100 million US jobs are exposed to automation, covering fast food, customer service and manual labour, but also accounting, software development and nursing. Senator Mark Warner has warned recent graduates could face unemployment near 25% within three years.Hinton's fog is still there. The 175,479 tech jobs cut in this year are not, and the names on that list run through Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, and plenty of others.
Article Summary: Geoffrey Hinton says the real problem is nobody left to buy what AI makes. Musk has said most people won't have to work at all inside two decades. Bill Gates has suggested humans may soon not be needed for most things. Hinton accepts the first half and rejects the second.

Article Title: As iPhone 18 series launch nears, one of Tesla’s biggest investor Ross Gerber says that ‘now is a good time’ to buy iPhone 17 as Apple …
Article Text:
iOS 27 beta 5 reportedly lists six unreleased iPhones

What Tesla’s biggest investor Ross Gerber said

Apple iPhone 18 could face higher costs

Apple’s pricing strategy

Ross Gerber, co-founder, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management and one of Tesla's most prominent individual investors is now telling consumers that if they are in the market for a new iPhone, then they may want to move before Apple ’s next-generation lineup arrives. In a post shared on X (formerly known as Twitter) Gerber said that Apple’s iPhone 17 sales remain robust despite rising hardware prices. “In the Apple Store, they told me sales are as good as ever even with higher prices,” Gerber posted on X.In a post on X over the weekend, Gerber said iPhone sales remain strong despite rising prices across Apple's broader hardware lineup, noting that staff at an Apple Store told him sales were as good as ever even with higher pricing elsewhere in the product range. He pointed out that Apple has held the iPhone 17's price steady so far, and suggested that anyone considering a new iPhone 17 might want to buy now rather than wait.The iPhone 17 currently starts at $799 for the 256GB model in the U.S., with the iPhone 17 Pro starting at $1,099 and the iPhone 17 Pro Max at $1,199.“In the Apple Store, they told me sales are as good as ever even with higher prices. The current iPhone 17 price has not gone up but it will in September with the new models… so current iPhone sales are quite good. If you’re looking for a new iPhone 17… now is a good time. $AAPL,” wrote Gerber.Industry analysts warn that the upcoming iPhone 18 may carry higher costs due to soaring memory prices. TrendForce estimates the bill of materials for the 256GB iPhone 18 Pro could rise by 38% compared with the iPhone 17 Pro. Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management has predicted Apple could raise prices by about $125, or 15%.Apple has already raised prices across several products — including MacBooks, iPads, HomePods, and Apple TV — while keeping iPhone pricing unchanged. The company has warned that surging DRAM and storage costs are pressuring margins. Despite this, iPhone revenue in Apple’s fiscal third quarter reached $54.25 billion, up from $44.58 billion a year earlier, underscoring continued demand.
Article Summary: Ross Gerber, co-founder, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management, is one of Tesla's most prominent individual investors. In a post shared on X (formerly known as Twitter) Gerber said that Apple’s iPhone 17 sales remain robust despite rising hardware prices. Apple has already raised prices across several products — including MacBooks, iPads, HomePods, and Apple TV — while keeping iPhone pricing unchanged.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences







In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. The sale was based on economic and political reasons. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: 1 in 3 registered voters to be out of Delhi’s draft poll roll; list out on Aug 24
Article Text:
Election officials said nearly 75% of the over 47 lakh voters are those who seem to have shifted (either within the city or outside). (Representative image)

Stats now

What to do in case name is missing





NEW DELHI: One in three registered voters in Delhi will not find their name in the draft electoral roll that will be published on Aug 24.The names of 47.6 lakh registered voters, out of the city’s 1.45 crore electorate, or 33%, have not found place in Delhi’s draft electoral rolls under the ongoing special intensive revision (SIR) as the door-to-door verification drive came to a close Monday.The draft roll will be published on Aug 24. Those who live in the city but find their names missing will have a month to get their names added to the rolls again after fresh application and verification.The verification drive, undertaken by 13,000 booth-level officers, lasted a month and a half. Officials said those who failed to submit their forms for verification will be dropped from the draft roll.Election officials said nearly 75% of the over 47 lakh voters are those who seem to have shifted (either within the city or outside).By Monday, forms of nearly 97.5 lakh of the 1.45 crore voters were verified and their records had been digitised, taking the overall verification of enumeration forms rate to 67.2%.At 6pm, only 2,542 enumeration forms were yet to be verified and digitised, which means that the change in the number of voters who are set to be dropped will be marginal.In Jan 2025, days before the Delhi assembly polls, the city had 1.55 crore registered voters.Before SIR began, this number had dropped to 1.45 crore. Election officials said this was due to “a continuous process” of updating the voter list.An official said one of the key reasons behind the large deletion is that many people have moved houses.“People frequently shift houses within Delhi, move to neighbouring NCR cities such as Noida, Ghaziabad, Gurgaon and Faridabad, or relocate to far-off areas due to work, family or other reasons. It has been observed that many people don’t update their addresses in the voter card and that is why they were not found at their addresses even though the booth-level officers visited their homes multiple times,” said the poll official.Registered voters whose names are not included in the draft SIR roll will get a month to get their names included if they still live in Delhi.“They will have to apply for fresh voter card by submitting Form 6. Voters can file claims and objections from Aug 24 to Sept 23, including Form 6 for enrolment at a new address. After verification, eligible voters will be included in the final electoral roll on Oct 27,” said an official.SIR was launched in Delhi on June 30 to verify and update the capital’s electoral rolls and ensure that no eligible citizen is left out, while ineligible voters such as those who have moved out of the city are weeded out. Originally scheduled to end on July 29, SIR was extended twice.During SIR’s enumeration phase, 13,000 BLOs distributed 100% of the forms in 13 districts, the office of Delhi’s chief election officer said.Outer North district recorded the highest digitisation at 75.7%, with 6.3 lakh of its 8.3 lakh forms digitised. West followed at 73.3%, with 10.7 lakh of 14.6 lakh forms digitised. South West recorded a digitisation rate of 73.2%.North East, which has the highest number of electors, digitised 13.3 lakh of the 18.7 lakh forms distributed, taking its rate to 70.9%. North West was marginally behind at 70.9%.At the lower end, South East recorded the lowest digitisation rate at 56.3%, with 8.7 lakh of 15.6 lakh forms digitised. New Delhi stood at 60.8%, while South recorded 61.3%. Central recorded 61.9%, North 64.1%, East 64.4%, Old Delhi 66.9% and Central North 68.8%.
Article Summary: One in three registered voters in Delhi will not find their name in the draft electoral roll that will be published on Aug 24. Names of 47.6 lakh registered voters, or 33%, have not found place in Delhi’s draft electoral rolls under the ongoing special intensive revision (SIR) Those who live in the city but find their names missing will have a month to get their names added to the rolls again.

Article Title: 13 years, repeated AIIMS visits, but heart surgery still eludes Kota girl
Article Text:
TOI

TOI





New Delhi: A 15-year-old Kota girl has been visiting AIIMS Delhi since she was two for a congenital heart defect, but her father alleges that despite repeated consultations and surgery dates, the corrective procedure never took place.Tanvi was first brought to AIIMS on Oct 10, 2012, when she was two. Her records document ventricular septal defect (VSD). Her father, Mukesh Pariyani, alleges that doctors discussed surgery to close the defect and address the pulmonary artery.An AIIMS estimate certificate dated Jan 31, 2014 records her diagnosis as “VSD + pulmonary atresia” and lists “unifocalisation & conduit” as the surgery required. It estimated the cost at Rs 1.25 lakh and mentioned four blood donors. Four replacement blood donor cards are also in the file.Pariyani said the surgery date of Sept 2, 2015, was given and later changed to Nov 16, but the procedure did not take place. He also said that a person named Sanjeev, whom he described as an implant/drug company representative, took Rs 30,000 from him for implants. The allegation could not be independently verified.The records show Tanvi was being followed in CTVS under Dr Sachin Talwar.The AIIMS grievance response in 2016 advised the family to meet Dr Talwar for “further evaluation and management of surgery.”A 2018 assessment found some major blood vessels to the lungs were absent and described her heart anatomy as complex. Further evaluation was advised.Dr Talwar toldthat Tanvi is not a candidate for surgery because the arteries supplying blood to her lungs are essentially absent. He said he had reviewed her CT scans multiple times, discussed the case with the family and documented his assessment in her records. “If the anatomy is not amenable to surgery, it is better for the patient to live for whatever time they have,” the doctor said.Tanvi’s father toldthat she has had recurrent fever, cough and cold for the last one-and-a-half years, has lost weight and become weak, and has been unable to attend school in recent weeks. He said he was frustrated after years of making the rounds of AIIMS and wanted an opportunity to discuss the case directly with Dr Talwar.In a June 2025 grievance, he said his daughter was awaiting surgery and he could not afford treatment elsewhere. The complaint was marked as under process and referred to AIIMS.The father again approached PMO in Feb 2026, alleging that despite complaints in 2016 and 2025, no action had been taken and that his daughter’s condition was deteriorating. The grievance remained to be under process.This is not the first case of a minor whose cardiac surgery at AIIMS has faced a prolonged delay.TOI had earlier reported the case of Aayansh Kumar, a Bihar boy whose surgery was delayed for nearly six years despite being given surgery dates repeatedly.Aayansh was being treated by the same doctor, Dr Sachin Talwar, and was operated upon at AIIMS in June 2024 after his family’s plight was highlighted in these columns.When contacted, AIIMS media cell in-charge, professor Rima Dada, said: “It is a matter of concern. The matter will be looked into and resolved.”The case also brings into focus the Supreme Court’s recognition of healthcare as part of the right to life under Article 21. In Surjit Singh vs State of Punjab (1996), the court held that self-preservation of life is a necessary concomitant of the right to life.
Article Summary: Tanvi was first brought to AIIMS on Oct 10, 2012, when she was two. Her records document ventricular septal defect (VSD) Her father, Mukesh Pariyani, alleges that doctors discussed surgery to close the defect.

Article Title: Actress Rupa Dutta gets bail in Rs 1.48L Colaba theft case
Article Text:
Bengali actor Rupa Dutta received bail from a Mumbai court last week





MUMBAI: A Metropolitan Magistrate's Court granted bail to 43-year-old Bengali actor Rupa Umashankar Dutta, who was arrested last week for allegedly stealing valuables worth Rs 1.48 lakh in Colaba. Rupa Dutta is an actress who has worked in a few Hindi and Bengali movies, including 'Sathi'.She has also worked in the Hindi serial, 'Jai Maa Vaishnodevi', apart from some Bengali films. She made headlines in 2022, when she was first arrested for pickpocketing at the Kolkata Book Fair in 2022.RS Bhosale (Narsale), additional chief judicial Magistrate, granted bail to Dutta on a personal bond of Rs 50,000 and directed that she shall not tamper with the evidence or leave India without court's permission.The case pertains to a complaint lodged by a Marine Drive-resident Dimple Singhvi, who lodged a complaint with the Colaba police that her purse containing a diamond-studded gold bracelet worth Rs 1.20 lakh, cash of Rs 10,000, Apple AirPods worth Rs 15,000, a wallet and other personal documents were stolen on July 12, 2026, while she was moving through crowded areas between Babulnath Temple and Colaba.During probe, Colaba Police stumbled upon CCTV footage where Dutta is seen tailing the victim. On July 6, police arrested Rupa. Some of the stolen property was also recovered from her possession. Her advocate Sunil Pandey argued that the accused had been falsely implicated and was a victim of circumstances.
Article Summary: Bengali actor Rupa Umashankar Dutta, 43, was arrested last week for allegedly stealing valuables worth Rs 1.48 lakh in Colaba. She made headlines in 2022, when she was first arrested for pickpocketing at the Kolkata Book Fair in 2022. Her advocate Sunil Pandey argued that the accused had been falsely implicated.
